Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money changes hands. If you do a job in June and send an invoice, accrual books show the sale in June even if the client pays in July. Similarly, if you get supplies now but pay next month, the cost is recorded now. Cash-basis accounting waits until money actually arrives or leaves your bank: the sale and the bill show up only when you get paid or when you pay.

Accrual gives a clearer picture of how your business is doing over time because it ties work and costs to the same period. Cash basis is simpler and easier to follow since it tracks actual cash flow. Small businesses often use cash basis for simplicity, while businesses that want more complete financial information choose accrual. Choose the one that best fits your size and needs. Talk to your accountant if unsure.

Accrual and cash-basis accounting differ mainly in timing. Cash-basis records income when you actually receive cash and records expenses when you actually pay. It’s simple and shows your immediate cash on hand. Accrual accounting records income when you earn it (for example, when you deliver a product or send an invoice) and records expenses when you incur them (for example, when you receive a bill), even if cash comes later. That means accrual shows what was truly earned and spent during a period, while cash-basis shows what cash moved. Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing profitability; cash-basis makes it easier to track short-term cash flow. Small operations often use cash-basis for simplicity; businesses that need a fuller view of performance usually use accrual. Accrual and cash-basis accounting are two ways to record money in and out, and they tell different stories about a business.

Cash-basis: You record income when you actually get paid and record expenses when you actually pay bills. It’s simple and shows how much cash you have on hand, but it can hide whether the business really earned that money or owes costs later.

Accrual-basis: You record income when you earn it (even if the customer hasn’t paid yet) and record expenses when you incur them (even if you haven’t paid the bill). This approach matches sales and the costs that made those sales, so it gives a clearer picture of profits and ongoing performance. However, it can make you look profitable while lacking cash to pay bills.

Which to use depends on complexity and needs: cash-basis for simplicity and cash focus; accrual-basis for a more accurate view of business performance over time.
